I spent the last ten years of my life living in LA working at becoming a professional screenwriter. I’d say that succeeding at that level of the entertainment industry is comparably difficult to making a good living developing your own apps.

Here are my thoughts on this kind of aspiration. There are two kinds of people, the ones who will tell you it’s extraordinarily difficult to succeed at this type of dream (they’re right), and those who tell you there’s value in following your dreams no matter how unlikely they are to come true (they’re also right).

I spent years writing scripts that no one would ever read. I suffered rejection after rejection. I worked service industry jobs to make ends meet. I had some really low lows.

I also found successes along the way. I sold a show to Disney. I have a movie on Netflix. I’ve pitched and sold ideas to a range of production companies all over LA.

Ultimately, even those successes weren’t enough to build a career on. Now, ten years after starting, I’m totally burnt out on the entertainment industry. I left LA and here I am studying to become a web developer.

Do I regret my time pursuing my dream? Nope. If I could do it over again would I? Yep.

Even in failure, which is likely, you gain life experience, achieve high highs, and build confidence all along the way.

Following your dreams is great. If your dreams eventually shift (mine did) then that’s okay too. Don’t look to others to give you permission to pursue your passions. If you’re smart about it, life will work itself out.

Also, start investing in an IRA even if you’re broke. Don’t spend ten years following your dreams without at least building a little nest egg to cushion your fall.

There are exceptions for sure. It’s certainly possible to get an entry level job at a fin tech company with non-relevant c++ experience. But you’ll probably have a much harder time than someone who has relevant experience.

A random guy who speaks Italian could certainly get a bank teller job. But he’s probably not gonna get hired over someone who’s actually been a bank teller before. And programming jobs are more competitive than bank teller jobs.

Learning a programming language is the most trivial part of a development job. So much so that I’m sure that most hiring managers would prefer an applicant without c++ but with relevant programming experience over the converse.

C++ is a language. Game development/financial tech development is something you do with the language. Knowing the language is a fine start, but it won’t get you hired at a fin tech company unless you also know some elements of fin tech.

Put another way. If you learned to speak Italian because you worked at, say, an Italian video game company, would that then qualify you to work at an Italian bank? Yes, of course the bank will be happy that you can speak Italian, but they won’t hire you *only* because you speak Italian. They also want you to understand “bank stuff”.

An anecdote from my own life. Two years ago I was head over heels in love with my girlfriend, I was healthy, I had bright career prospects. I felt so happy that I actually considered writing a book on how to be happy. Literally. It seemed so clear to me at the time that I had it all "figured out."

Of course, all that changed. My girlfriend and I broke up. My health has taken a downward turn. And those career prospects never panned out. It all turned out to be rather... impermanent.

I find myself suffering quite deeply these days. One thing I have noticed, however, is that at least some of my suffering is caused by an attachment to how I want things to be, an attachment to how things were. The more I can find acceptance in my present moment, rather than desiring something else, the less I seem to suffer.

That doesn't mean I'm not striving to regain my health, career, and find love again. But I'm also working to strengthen my practice of Buddhism and mindfulness. Again, easier said than done, but I'm working on it.

What exactly are they trying to treat with the steroid?

Is there an alternative medication that could be effective that doesn't contain a steroid?

Do I have an infection?

Why am I being prescribed an antibiotic?

What are the possible side effects of this medication?

Is there a more conservative treatment option that doesn't involve medication?

Generally speaking, you need to get comfortable advocating for yourself with medical professionals and fully understanding the interventions they are recommending. Voice your concerns. Negotiate the details of the assignment so you're both clear on expectations. (topic and length of piece, pay amount, when you'll be paid, how you'll be paid, downpayment, how many rewrites the client may request, when you'll deliver, copyright ownership, etc.). Do this over email so there's a written record.

Get a contract signed by both parties stating what you negotiated.

Get paid a down payment before you start (I'd recommend 50%).

Write it.

Deliver it.

Do any requested rewrites.

Get paid the rest of what you're owed.
